summary: Phenindione is an oral indanedione vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant used to treat and prevent venous and arterial thromboembolism. It is not FDA-approved; this record is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF. Dose is fully individualized to the INR (commonly target 2.0-3.0). Although effective, phenindione has been largely superseded by warfarin because of serious and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reactions - including rash, hepatitis, interstitial nephritis/nephropathy and agranulocytosis - usually appearing in the first weeks of treatment. It characteristically and harmlessly colors the urine pink, red or orange, which should be explained to patients to avoid alarm. Bleeding is the principal dose-related risk; reversal is with vitamin K and, for major bleeds, prothrombin complex concentrate.
indications: Treatment and prevention of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism)
Prevention of thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation
Prevention of thromboembolism in other high-risk conditions, generally where warfarin is unsuitable or not tolerated

dosage.d: Approximately 200 mg on day 1 and 100 mg on day 2, then adjust by INR (lower in elderly/at-risk)
dosage.n: Avoid excessive loading; check INR early and watch for early hypersensitivity

dosage.d: Usually ~25-100 mg/day titrated to the target INR (commonly 2.0-3.0)
dosage.t: Once daily or in divided doses
dosage.n: Never fixed-dose; titrate strictly to INR

dosage.c: Elderly / hepatic or renal impairment / high bleeding risk
dosage.d: Lower starting and maintenance dose with cautious titration
Overlap and dose per local anticoagulation protocol with INR guidance
dosage.n: Warfarin is generally preferred; reserve phenindione for warfarin-intolerant patients

admin: Take once daily at the same time each day so INR results can guide same-day dose changes
Dose is set entirely by INR - never use a fixed dose without monitoring
Maintain a consistent dietary vitamin K intake (green leafy vegetables); avoid large swings
Avoid binge alcohol and review every new medicine for interactions
Warn the patient that urine may turn pink/red/orange - this is harmless and not blood
Carry an anticoagulant alert card and inform all clinicians/dentists before procedures
moa: Phenindione inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of reduced vitamin K. This impairs gamma-carboxylation and hence the synthesis of functional vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S), producing a delayed anticoagulant effect once pre-formed factors are cleared. It is an indanedione derivative rather than a coumarin.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to phenindione or other indanediones
Pregnancy - teratogenic and risk of fetal/neonatal hemorrhage
Severe hepatic disease with coagulopathy / esophageal varices
Recent or planned surgery on the CNS or eye; conditions with high hemorrhage risk
relative: Peptic ulcer disease or history of GI bleeding
Poor adherence or inability to monitor INR
Availability of warfarin (generally preferred due to better safety profile)
monitor: Hypersensitivity: rash, fever, sore throat, jaundice; full blood count and LFTs/renal function early in treatment

preg: Contraindicated - like other vitamin K antagonists, phenindione crosses the placenta and can cause embryopathy and fetal/neonatal bleeding and CNS abnormalities. Use heparin/LMWH instead during pregnancy where anticoagulation is required.
lact: Avoid - phenindione is excreted in breast milk in amounts that may cause hemorrhage in the infant; if anticoagulation is needed during breastfeeding, warfarin (considered safer in milk) is generally preferred.
renal: Use with caution; monitor INR more closely as anticoagulant response and bleeding risk may be increased. Avoid in significant renal impairment, and be alert for drug-induced interstitial nephritis/nephropathy as part of the hypersensitivity syndrome.
hepatic: The anticoagulant effect is enhanced in hepatic impairment (reduced clotting-factor synthesis and altered drug metabolism); contraindicated in severe liver disease with coagulopathy and used cautiously with close INR monitoring otherwise. Hepatitis can also occur as a hypersensitivity reaction.

major: Drugs increasing bleeding/INR: NSAIDs, aspirin, other anticoagulants/antiplatelets, azole antifungals (fluconazole, miconazole), metronidazole, cotrimoxazole, amiodarone, many antibiotics
Enzyme inducers decreasing effect (risk of clotting): rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates, St John's wort
moderate: Statins, fibrates, thyroid hormones - can potentiate effect
minor: Many other drugs alter INR - review every new medication
interactions.food: Maintain consistent vitamin K intake; large amounts of green leafy vegetables or sudden dietary change can lower INR.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid binge drinking; acute alcohol raises INR/bleeding risk and chronic heavy use can lower it - keep intake low and consistent.
interactions.diagnostics: Prolongs INR/prothrombin time (the basis of monitoring); affects coagulation assays. Pink/red/orange discoloration of urine is a drug effect, not hematuria, and may confuse urinalysis.

common: Pink, red or orange discoloration of the urine (harmless drug effect)
serious: Hypersensitivity reactions: severe rash/exfoliative dermatitis, fever, hepatitis, interstitial nephritis/nephropathy
Agranulocytosis / leukopenia and other blood dyscrasias
Skin necrosis (early, especially with protein C/S deficiency)
rare: Myocarditis or pericarditis as part of hypersensitivity
emergency: Signs of intracranial hemorrhage (severe headache, weakness, altered consciousness)
Severe hypersensitivity reaction (widespread rash with fever, jaundice, sore throat suggesting agranulocytosis)

monitoring: INR regularly - frequently at initiation and after any dose/drug/diet change, then at stable intervals
Hypersensitivity surveillance early in therapy: skin, fever, sore throat, jaundice, with full blood count, LFTs and renal function
Review of new medicines and dietary vitamin K consistency
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed at the same time daily and never change the dose without an INR result
Your urine may turn pink, red or orange - this is a harmless effect of the medicine and is not blood; mention it if you are worried
Stop and seek medical advice urgently if you develop a rash, fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers or yellowing of the skin/eyes (signs of a serious reaction)
Report unusual bleeding or bruising, black stools or a severe headache at once
Tell every doctor, dentist and pharmacist that you take an anticoagulant before any procedure or new medicine, and carry an alert card
pk: Anticoagulant effect begins ~24-48 h (delay until clotting factors fall)
Plasma peak within a few hours; full INR effect after 1-2 days
Anticoagulant effect lasts ~1-3 days after stopping
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved (this record is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF); an indanedione rather than a coumarin
Largely superseded by warfarin because of serious hypersensitivity reactions (rash, hepatitis, nephropathy, agranulocytosis), typically in the first weeks - reserve for warfarin-intolerant patients
Characteristically turns urine pink/red/orange - a harmless effect that should be explained to avoid alarm and not mistaken for hematuria
Dose is ENTIRELY INR-guided (commonly target 2.0-3.0); never fixed-dose
Reverse with vitamin K (phytomenadione); use prothrombin complex concentrate (not just FFP) for major bleeding
missed: Take a missed dose on the same day if remembered; if not remembered until the next day, skip it and do NOT double up. Record the missed dose and tell the anticoagulation clinic, as it can affect the INR.
overdose: Overdose causes excessive anticoagulation and bleeding. Management depends on INR and bleeding: omit doses for minor over-anticoagulation; give oral/IV vitamin K (phytomenadione) for high INR; and for major bleeding give prothrombin complex concentrate (or fresh frozen plasma if unavailable) plus IV vitamin K, with supportive care.
